title: Transformer scarcity pays the equipment makers, not the event study
payer: equipment makers collect pricing power, developers and ratepayers pay for it in delay and cost
why_now: grid capex is rising while heavy equipment capacity is fixed, and our own event study already showed the delay is not tradable through the developer

links.claim: Interconnection and energization require large power transformers and high-voltage gear with multi-year procurement queues.
links.assumption: The lead time is a queue, not a price, so it cannot be cleared by paying more in the short run.
links.kill: Lead times shorten while order books stay full and prices fall.
links.source: supplier disclosures, trade press, Wood Mackenzie and ICF commentary

links.claim: Scarcity in a queue market shows up first as price and allocation power for the equipment makers.
links.assumption: OEMs can hold price because capacity cannot be added inside two years.
links.kill: Transformer price indices fall while backlogs rise.
links.source: BLS PPI transformers, USITC import unit values, supplier price commentary

links.claim: Pricing power converts into margins and free cash flow when large projects ship, years after booking.
links.assumption: Margin is not competed away by Siemens, Hitachi, GE Vernova, and new entrants before delivery.
links.kill: Backlog converts at flat or falling margins.

links.claim: The payer is the developer and ultimately the ratepayer, so the same mechanism that makes our delivery tail negative for the developer is positive for the supplier.
links.assumption: Cost escalation lands on the developer's schedule and budget, not on the OEM's penalty clauses.
links.kill: Liquidated damages absorb the delay cost at the OEM.
links.source: EPC and supply agreements in 8-K filings

links.claim: The edge is cross-sectional: whether this is priced depends on relative, not absolute, valuation.
links.assumption: The market has not fully capitalised the queue economics into supplier multiples, or has capitalised it unevenly.
links.kill: Supplier forward multiples already rank the same way as the backlog quality measure.
links.source: none; this is the chain's greatest assumption and the study must treat it as the null

title: Grain-oriented steel is the transformer core bottleneck
payer: steel makers with GOES capacity collect rent while transformer output is capped
why_now: transformer capacity additions depend on a narrow class of electrical steel that few mills make

nodes_to_add.meaning: grain-oriented electrical steel used in transformer cores

links.claim: Transformer cores need grain-oriented electrical steel, produced by a small set of mills.
links.assumption: No substitute material qualifies for the large units on the critical path.
links.kill: Amorphous or alternative core designs take share in large units.

links.claim: GOES capacity additions are slow and lumpy, so transformer output cannot outrun steel supply.
links.assumption: GOES, not copper, labor or winding capacity, is the binding input in practice.
links.kill: Transformer output rises while GOES supply is flat, for example through imports that fill the gap.
links.source: USITC trade data, mill expansion announcements

links.claim: When the binding input is scarce, its price and allocation power rise before the downstream product price does.
links.assumption: Contracts reprice within a year rather than riding long-term fixed prices.
links.kill: GOES contract prices stay flat through a scarcity episode.
links.source: import unit values, producer price indices

links.claim: The observable is import volumes and unit values by origin, joined to transformer shipment data.
links.assumption: Customs codes separate GOES from other flat steel well enough to measure it.
links.kill: The HS line is too broad to isolate GOES.

title: Turbine slot scarcity delays entry and tightens the local power market
payer: merchant generators with existing capacity collect the scarcity; late entrants pay for it
why_now: gas plant orders are queued behind a fixed turbine supply while load growth is real and local

links.claim: New gas capacity requires turbine slots that are allocated years ahead.
links.assumption: Slot holders cannot flip slots to faster projects when prices rise.
links.kill: Slot trading accelerates projects enough to keep dates.
links.source: turbine OEM backlog disclosures, trade press

links.claim: Delayed entry shows up as slipped commercial operation dates in the planned inventory.
links.assumption: Our planned-sheet revision measure captures this class of slip, which our panels already track.
links.kill: Gas projects slip for reasons that never reach the planned sheet.

links.claim: When entry slips in a node with rising load, reserve margins tighten and forward power prices rise.
links.assumption: The local market is tight enough that a two-year slip matters, rather than being covered by imports or demand response.
links.kill: Reserve margins hold while entry slips, or prices fall.
links.source: ISO capacity auctions, EIA-930, forward power curves

links.claim: Existing merchant capacity in that node earns the scarcity, and the payer is the load that cannot move.
links.assumption: Scarcity rents are not fully hedged away in advance.
links.kill: Hedges and contracts pass the scarcity through to consumers immediately.

title: Interconnection upgrade costs push marginal projects out, and the exit shows up in supplier books
payer: developers eat the study cost; equipment makers whose slots were reserved absorb the cancellation
why_now: the measured withdrawal share is already 57 percent across the queue, and the cost of the upgrade decision is the clearest reason a marginal project leaves

links.claim: Cluster studies assign network upgrade costs that can exceed a project's economics.
links.assumption: Upgrade costs are not socialised enough to save marginal projects.
links.kill: Cost allocation reforms move the burden to ratepayers at scale.
links.source: ISO cluster study reports, LBNL Queued Up

links.claim: When the assigned cost crosses the project's threshold, the rational move is withdrawal, which our queue panel already measures at 57.4 percent.
links.assumption: Withdrawals are economically driven, not housekeeping of duplicate applications.
links.kill: Withdrawals cluster in projects with trivial upgrade costs.

links.claim: Withdrawn projects had reserved long-lead equipment, so the cancellation reaches supplier order books with a lag.
links.assumption: Reservations are real and cancellable, not options that were never booked into backlog.
links.kill: Backlogs are unaffected by queue exit waves.

links.claim: A queue exit wave is therefore an early observable for supplier guidance risk in the affected segment.
links.assumption: The market does not price the exit wave until the supplier discloses it, which is the greatest assumption here and the study's null.
links.kill: Supplier multiples move with our queue-exit series at the same time, with no lag.
links.source: results/queue-panel.csv joined to supplier event windows

title: Cooling water constraints push data-center siting, and the counterexample is loud
payer: utilities in water-stressed service areas lose the load, or pay to build the water side
why_now: large-scale computing consumes water for cooling in regions that are also the cheapest power and are drying

links.claim: Evaporative cooling consumes water at a scale that matters in stressed basins.
links.assumption: Water use stays large, rather than shifting to closed-loop or air cooling designs.
links.kill: New builds shift to designs with negligible water use at scale.
links.source: operator sustainability reports, utility water filings

links.claim: Some regions limit new consumption through permits, discharge rules and aquifer constraints.
links.assumption: Permitting actually binds before land and power do.
links.kill: Sites announce and build in the most constrained basins anyway; Phoenix and the desert buildout are the standing counterexample.

links.claim: When siting is blocked or delayed, the local load growth path and the utility capex tied to it weaken.
links.assumption: The delayed load does not simply move to another state in the same utility's footprint.
links.kill: Load reappears elsewhere in the same balanced area.

links.claim: This chain is kept as a watch item because its own kill test is a known live counterexample, which is exactly the honest reason not to trade it.
links.assumption: None of the above is decided; the chain's value is that it names the permit data that would decide it.
links.kill: A permit-level dataset shows water constraints delaying projects relative to matched peers.
links.source: to fetch: county permit records, USGS water data

title: The electrician pipeline, not the equipment, may be the binding schedule constraint
payer: contractors with crews price the scarcity; developers absorb the schedule
why_now: equipment queues are public and discussed, while the workforce that installs it is not

links.claim: Substation, line and data-center electrical work needs certified crews that take years to train.
links.assumption: Crews do not move freely across regions fast enough to clear local scarcity.
links.kill: Regional wage premia stay flat while schedules slip.

links.claim: Where crews are binding, schedules slip even when equipment arrives on time.
links.assumption: The slippage is separable from equipment delay in project disclosures.
links.kill: Projects disclose equipment, not labor, as the delay cause.

links.claim: The tradeable payer is the contractor with regional density, whose margins hold up while the pipeline is long.
links.assumption: Contractor margins are visible in segment reporting rather than buried in consolidated numbers.
links.kill: Contractor margins fall through the buildout.

title: Cheap power makes aluminum, expensive power unmakes it, and conductors gate the grid
payer: smelters with hedged power collect; cable and conductor buyers pay
why_now: power price spikes curtail smelting, and the same buildout needs aluminium conductor at scale

nodes_to_add.meaning: aluminium rod and conductor used in transmission and distribution build

links.claim: Aluminium smelting is a power contract business that curtails when power resale beats smelting.
links.assumption: Curtailment decisions respond to spot and forward power within a quarter.
links.kill: Smelters run through price spikes because contracts are fully hedged.

links.claim: Curtailment removes conductor supply exactly when the grid buildout raises conductor demand.
links.assumption: Other regions expand smelting output fast enough to fill the gap, which is the thing to test.
links.kill: Conductor prices and lead times stay flat through curtailment episodes.
links.source: LME and regional premia, cable maker order books

links.claim: The observable is smelter curtailment announcements joined to conductor lead times and cable maker backlogs.
links.assumption: Curtailment announcements are dated precisely enough to align with lead times.
links.kill: The announcement dates cannot be reconstructed point in time.

title: Funding cost reaches schedules only through the marginal developer
why_now: the whole complex is capital intensive and was financed through a low-rate window, and our panels live inside that window

links.claim: Project economics in this complex are rate sensitive because the cash flows start years out.
links.assumption: Developers re-underwrite on rate moves rather than ride fixed-rate project debt.
links.kill: Financing is locked at fixed rates for the life of the projects under study.

links.claim: Higher funding costs push marginal projects over the hurdle, converting into deferral and cancellation.
links.assumption: The marginal project is rate-limited rather than queue-limited or equipment-limited.
links.kill: Cancellations track queue and equipment constraints, not financing.

links.claim: Our windows cannot test this: the delivery panels run through the low-rate period, so a rate-regime test needs data this repo does not have yet.
links.assumption: The honest move is to park the chain rather than fit it on one regime.
links.kill: A second regime with enough events is assembled and the association disappears.

title: Load growth fills regulated rate base, if regulators allow it
payer: ratepayers pay the return; utility shareholders collect it if the case is allowed
why_now: load growth forecasts in data-center regions turned up after two decades of flat demand

links.claim: Regulated utilities earn a return on capital invested, so load growth converts into capex plans and rate base growth.
links.assumption: The regulatory compact holds and capital is recovered with a fair return.
links.kill: Rate cases start disallowing the demand-driven capex at scale.
links.source: rate case dockets, utility capex guidance

links.claim: Load growth is observable in balancing-authority demand before it becomes capex, which gives the ordering variable.
links.assumption: The demand growth is load-driven and persistent rather than weather or temporary timing.
links.kill: Growth is a weather artifact that reverses.

links.claim: The payer side has a political limit: large load growth raises rates for other customers, which invites pushback.
links.assumption: The pushback shows up in specific jurisdictions before it shows up in valuations.
links.kill: Rate outcomes stay uniformly constructive while bills rise.

links.claim: The edge is jurisdictional dispersion: the same load signal maps to different allowed outcomes by state.
links.assumption: The market prices the dispersion in one direction, which is the study's null.
links.kill: Utility multiples already rank the jurisdictions the way the analysis would.
links.source: rate case databases joined to utility equity returns

title: The revision to cash-flow chain, where our own null lives
payer: the developer's cash flow moves; the question is who agreed to pay for the delay
why_now: we measured this chain and the pricing half already failed on our panels, so the chain's value now is the exposure map, not the event study

links.claim: A promise revision delays the revenue of the project, which changes the developer's cash-flow timing.
links.assumption: The revision is material to reported periods rather than a rounding of the schedule.
links.kill: Large revisions arrive with no measurable cash-flow disclosure.

links.claim: Who pays for the delay is written in the contract: fixed-price EPC passes it to the contractor, cost-plus keeps it with the developer.
links.assumption: Contract type is distinguishable from filings.
links.kill: Contract structures do not change the incidence of delay cost.

links.claim: The equity pricing of the revision is already measured and null on our panels, so this link is closed rather than assumed.
links.assumption: The null generalises to the bigger revisions we can now see in the queue-matched subset.
links.kill: A larger tail sample overturns the null, in a fresh window.

links.claim: The remaining untested link is the contract incidence: the same revision should move the contractor's guidance differently than the developer's.
links.assumption: Contractor guidance reacts to delay cost at all, rather than being absorbed in a diversified book.
links.kill: Contractors guide through revisions without a measurable pattern.
links.source: contractor filings joined to dated revisions

title: The salmon chain, graded: sea temperature to harvest to the index
payer: integrated farmers with the best sites collect; feed costs and lice limits decide the margin
why_now: demonstration of the method on the captain's example, and an honest verdict on whether it belongs to this repo's venues

links.claim: Sea temperature drives farmed salmon growth rates and lice pressure, which together set harvest volumes.
links.assumption: Temperature is the leading driver among biology, regulation and feed.
links.kill: Harvest volumes follow regulatory lice limits and smolt release schedules with no temperature signal.
links.source: SSB harvest statistics, Nofima and BarentsWatch temperature series

links.claim: Wild catch and predator-prey dynamics move with the same ocean conditions, which is the captain's wider web.
links.assumption: The wild side is a separate supply channel rather than a substitute that stabilises price.
links.kill: Wild catch and farmed supply offset each other in price.

links.claim: Feed costs (soy, fishmeal, fish oil) set the margin against the harvest price.
links.assumption: Feed contracts reprice within the same horizon as the harvest signal.
links.kill: Feed costs are locked long enough to be irrelevant at the trading horizon.
links.source: feed producers' disclosures, futures for soy and fishmeal

links.claim: Demand is concentrated in Japanese sushi and US retail, where the cut and quality preferences decide which producer's fish clears at a premium.
links.assumption: Quality premia are producer-specific enough to separate margins.
links.kill: The index price is a commodity price with no producer-level dispersion.

links.claim: The instrument is Fish Pool futures or integrated farmer equity, and FX (NOK) sits between the harvest price and shareholder returns.
links.assumption: Futures liquidity and basis allow expression at the sizes the signal would justify.
links.kill: The contract is too illiquid to express the view net of costs.

links.claim: Verdict for this repo: watch item. It is a real chain with a testable core, but it needs data this repo does not have, and no node of ours touches it except through method.
links.assumption: The honest disposition is to record the grade and not pretend it is ours.
links.kill: A tie to one of our existing nodes appears, for example a feed commodity shared with a complex we trade.
links.source: none; disposition by the method's testability gate

title: Canal transit restrictions reach US power through gas
payer: US gas producers and power sellers see the flow shift; importers pay
why_now: an exotic physical constraint on shipping can move the same gas balances that set our complex's power prices

links.claim: Drought lowers canal water levels and cuts daily transit slots.
links.assumption: The restriction is not offset by booking auctions and rerouting at scale.
links.kill: Transit volumes recover through alternate routings and slot auctions.

links.claim: Reduced transits raise voyage times and freight cost for LNG and container flows between the Pacific and the Atlantic.
links.assumption: The affected routes cannot substitute Suez or the Cape without losing the arbitrage.
links.kill: Rerouting absorbs the restriction with no freight spread.

links.claim: When LNG routing shifts, US export pull and domestic gas balances shift with it.
links.assumption: US LNG flows are swing volumes sensitive to freight, which is the thing to test.
links.kill: US feedgas is unchanged through the restriction.
links.source: EIA LNG feedgas and export data

links.claim: Gas balances set power prices in the marginal market, which is the node our complex already depends on.
links.assumption: The marginal power market is gas-set through the episode.
links.kill: Power prices decouple from gas in the affected regions.

title: Insurance withdrawal reaches utility credit before it reaches capex
payer: utility security holders absorb liability; ratepayers absorb the recovery
why_now: physical risk is repricing insurance in the same regions that hold the grid capex we study

links.claim: Insurers are withdrawing from wildfire-exposed regions or repricing sharply.
links.assumption: Public utility commissions do not fully substitute for the insurance market.
links.kill: State backstops fill the gap at no cost to utilities.
links.source: state insurance department filings, carrier disclosures

links.claim: Uninsured liability risk raises the utility's cost of capital and narrows its financing capacity.
links.assumption: Rating agencies treat the exposure as a credit event rather than a tail scenario.
links.kill: Utility spreads do not move with insurance availability.

links.claim: A financing-constrained utility slows grid capex exactly when the buildout needs it.
links.assumption: Capex programs are financing-limited at the margin rather than pre-committed.
links.kill: Capex plans stay intact through credit stress.
links.source: utility capex guidance and financing plans

links.claim: The chain is a watch item for this repo: the dates are hard to align and the exposure is jurisdiction-specific, and the kill tests need insurance data we do not hold.
links.assumption: The honest disposition is to record the chain and name the data that would decide it.
links.kill: Insurance withdrawal dates joined to utility spread events show no pattern.
links.source: to fetch: state insurance filings, utility spread series
